title: Two Counters, One Cache Line: Sharing You Did Not Ask For

questions.question: Two threads increment two different atomic counters. The counters are moved from 8 bytes apart to 64. What happens?
options: It gets slower, because the data no longer fits in one line
It gets about six times faster, and nothing changes at 16 bytes because that is still one line
Nothing, since the counters were already separate variables
It gets about twice as fast, in proportion to the distance
questions.explanation: Measured: 159.0 ms at 8 bytes, 139.1 at 16, 27.1 at 64, 27.8 at 128. Caches move lines, not bytes, so two variables in one line are one thing to the hardware.

questions.question: Four threads each increment their own slot of a std::vector<std::atomic<long>>. Why is that slow?
options: The atomics use a lock internally
std::vector adds indirection to every access
Every slot is 8 bytes, so all four live in one line and four cores fight over it for the whole run
It is not slow; per-thread slots are the standard fix
questions.explanation: Measured at 162.1 ms packed against 34.8 with one slot per line, and 7.6 for a local on the stack published once at the end. A per-thread array is the most natural thing to write and it is the bug.

questions.question: Why put alignas on the type rather than a char array at the end of the struct?
options: There is no difference; both give sizeof 64
A trailing array gives the struct a size of 64 and no alignment
alignas is faster
A char array wastes more memory
questions.explanation: In a vector the first element can start part way through a line. sizeof says how far apart two elements are and nothing about where the first one starts. Both matter, and the test checks the distance between two elements of a real vector rather than reading the declaration.

questions.question: A queue's two indices are moved onto separate cache lines and throughput barely changes. Why?
options: The producer still reads the consumer's index on every push
The queue was not the bottleneck
The padding did not take effect
Separate lines are slower for small queues
questions.explanation: The line still moves; padding removed one of two reasons. Over four runs, padding alone was worth 1 to 6 percent and caching the other index alone was worth -8 to +14. The two together were worth 76, 77, 83 and 95 percent.

questions.question: What general rule comes out of that super-additive result?
options: Cache effects cannot be measured reliably
Always apply optimisations one at a time and keep the ones that measure
Padding should always be combined with locks
When an obviously correct fix produces no measurable improvement, something else is usually producing the same effect
questions.explanation: Measure combinations rather than changes. Removing one of two causes leaves the symptom exactly where it was, and the natural conclusion, that the fix was wrong, is the wrong conclusion.

questions.question: Should every shared variable be padded to a cache line?
options: No: a padded counter is 64 bytes instead of 8, so pad the few written by more than one thread and nothing else
No, padding never helps in practice
Yes, the compiler removes the padding when it is unnecessary
Yes, memory is cheap and correctness matters more
questions.explanation: For a handful of per-thread values the memory is nothing; for a million objects it is eight times the memory and a different problem. Not sharing the line at all, by accumulating in a local, is better still where it is available.
